faqs.q: I saw a snake near my Wellford home. Should I be worried?

Its wildlife work is orchard-and-lake work: raccoons and gray squirrels in the older homes and the canopy streets, groundhogs in the orchard banks and field edges, bats in the tall attics, and the lake's shoreline properties taking the raccoon and beaver pressure that standing water always delivers.

Inman.extendedBody:
Orchard banks and lake shore

Inman's ground calls follow its agriculture and its water. Groundhogs hold the sunny banks between the orchard rows and the roads, denning where the mowing stops — the same bank, re-let most springs if the openings stay. Beavers work the creeks and the lake's feeder branches, damming the slow reaches and backing water toward the low fields; their removal runs on the year-long depredation permit South Carolina issues for the species under §50-11-2570(A). Lake Bowen's shoreline homes add the dock-and-boathouse read: raccoons den in the structures over the water and commute the seawalls into the attics above them.

South Carolina's rules, applied in Inman

There is no SCDNR operator license — a referral list only — and any company advertising one is inventing a credential. Our Inman work runs on depredation permits for your property, with the handling rules attached: bats excluded by SCDNR's timing guidance, never sealed in with flightless pups; rabies-suspect animals reported through SC DPH. Older Inman homes hold big brown bat colonies in their tall attics, often for years; the exclusion that ends them is a complete map of the roofline's gaps, sealed in one programme when the timing is right.

In town: the historic read

Around the center, the work is the older housing stock's: open eaves, brick chimneys, addition junctions, and porches enclosed across the decades. We seal in metal fitted to the framing and cap the chimneys as a matter of course — in a small town, the finished jobs are visible from the street, and they are the reference the next call comes from.

Boiling Springs is Spartanburg's growth suburb — not a spring town anymore but one of the fastest-building communities in the upstate, wrapped around Lake Bowen's south shore and spreading subdivision by subdivision across the county's farm and orchard ground. Its wildlife work is the growth pattern at full strength: new phases pressed against standing woods and creek bottoms, displaced raccoons and armadillos in first-year attics and lawns, and the lake's established shoreline homes taking the older, steadier pressure — raccoons in the boathouses and attics, beavers in the feeder creeks, bats in the fascia of the 1970s lake houses now fifty years into their trim.

The two Boiling Springses need different inspections. The new streets need the boundary read — lot line against the woods, the creek bottom behind the phase, the construction details animals test first. The lake streets need the waterfront read — seawall, dock, boathouse, and the roofline above them as one structure. Our crews run both, and most Boiling Springs addresses turn out to need a weighted mix.
Boiling Springs.extendedBody:
Lake Bowen's shoreline system

On the lake, a home's wildlife defences start at the water. Raccoons den under docks and in boathouse voids, travel the seawall line, and reach the roof where the shore pines overhang; roof rats are not a Boiling Springs problem, but gray squirrels are, working the same canopy. We inspect and seal the system whole: boathouse and deck voids screened, roofline entries closed in metal, the tree bridges mapped for trimming. Sealing only the house on a lake lot solves the dry half of a wet problem. Beaver work runs in the feeder creeks on the year-long depredation permit (§50-11-2570(A)) — the permit structure South Carolina built for exactly this kind of seasonal water management.

Rules of the work in this state

South Carolina does not license wildlife operators; SCDNR's referral list is a listing, not a credential, and claims of a state license should end a hiring conversation. Removal runs on the depredation permit for your property, and its rules come with it — bats excluded on SCDNR's timing guidance, never sealed in while pups are flightless (the lake houses' free-tailed and big brown colonies are scheduled, not rushed), rabies-suspect animals reported through SC DPH. That framework, explained before the quote, is what there is to verify — ask for the explanation.

The growth edge

At the newest phases, the advice is the first-year perimeter inspection: crawlspace vents, garage corners, porch junctions, and the back lot line against the standing woods, closed while the work is small and the builder's warranty may still cover the failed detail. Displaced animals test new construction in its first season as a matter of routine; a sealed first-year house is simply not on their list.
